title: Restoring the Black Family: A Conversation with Delano Squires
author: Brad Wilcox and Delano Squires
source: Institute for Family Studies (ifstudies.org), November 4, 2026, November 6, 2026
summary: Brad Wilcox interviews Delano Squires about his book The Vanishing Black Family, which argues that welfare incentives and feminist cultural change made marriage optional for black Americans. Squires notes that while about 70 percent of black children are now born outside marriage, more than 75 percent were born to married parents in 1959 despite far higher poverty. He holds that AFDC and the growth of the welfare state made government a substitute husband, rewarding mothers for not marrying the father of their children. He adds that second-wave and black feminism cast marriage and men as obstacles, contrasting that with earlier black women writers such as Anna Julia Cooper who prized the home. For policy, he proposes using the bully pulpit, reporting indicators by family structure, success-sequence instruction in schools, and ideas like a newlywed investment account. Squires also urges black pastors to preach clearly about God's design for marriage and points to churches running marriage ministries.
points: Marriage among black Americans was far more common in 1959 than today despite higher poverty, which Squires uses to argue slavery and poverty alone do not explain the decline.
Squires argues that welfare programs such as AFDC acted as a substitute husband and created incentives against marrying the father of a woman's children.
He says second-wave and black feminism framed marriage and men as obstacles to liberation, in contrast with earlier pro-family black women writers.
Proposed steps include public messaging, reporting indicators by family structure, teaching the success sequence in schools and a newlywed savings account.
Churches are described as the key institution, with pastors urged to teach clearly on marriage and to build practical marriage ministries.
quotes: This means that in just three generations, a black child who is born to—and raised by—married parents went from being the norm to the exception.

While it is easy to blame slavery for the decline of marriage and increase in single-parent homes, the truth is that the family formation norms we see in black America today are the direct result of policy choices and cultural shifts that took place in the 1960s.
The expansion of welfare programs, particularly AFDC, made the federal government the de facto husband for millions of poor women across the country.

Welfare contributed to the destruction of the traditional family structure that was the norm in black America because it created powerful incentives for a woman not to marry the father of her children and instead depend on support from the government.

Elected officials should use every communication tool at their disposal (e.g., public remarks, awareness campaigns, social media) to consistently reinforce the evidence-based reality that children have the best outcomes when raised in a loving, safe, and secure home by their married biological parents.
The most important thing any pastor can do to support efforts to strengthen the family is preach with biblical clarity and conviction about God’s design for sex, sexuality, and marriage.

Both men give me hope that a revival of fatherhood and family is possible—for Americans of every race. But it will only be possible if pastors care more about rebuilding the family than retaking the White House.
